summary: Jordan Taylor's October 11, 2023 article argues that affordable housing should be a top local priority, describing a housing market where prices outpace incomes and the effects on families, schools and businesses. It reviews strategies including inclusionary zoning, tax incentives, land trusts, modular homes and new technology, along with grassroots advocacy, philanthropy and financing tools. It concludes that cross-sector partnerships and community input are key to inclusive, sustainable housing.
one_line: An opinion piece arguing that affordable housing needs coordinated community, government, private and nonprofit action, reviewing market conditions, strategies, funding and advocacy.
key_facts: The article "Ensuring Affordable Housing for All: A Community Imperative" was written by Jordan Taylor and dated October 11, 2023.
As of September 2023, real estate prices were outpacing average income growth by a substantial margin, according to the article.
The median home price in many urban areas exceeds seven times the median household income, a ratio that historically suggests severe unaffordability.
San Francisco, New York, and Los Angeles are cited as cities with a staggering deficit of available and accessible rental units for lower-income renters.
Educator Michael Johnson says that when families spend over 30% of their income on housing, it hurts their ability to invest in education, health care, and other essential services.
A Chamber of Commerce report released in August 2023 highlighted a sharp decline in workforce retention in areas with high living expenses.

Planning Commissioner Roberta Garcia says inclusionary zoning, which mandates a percentage of new construction be affordable units, "has helped, but it's not a silver bullet" and that renovation and preservation of existing affordable housing are also needed.
Other strategies named include tax incentives and subsidies for developers, land trusts run by nonprofits, and modular and prefabricated homes to reduce construction costs.
The "Homes for All" coalition in Denver, made up of citizens and non-profits, has lobbied for increased funding and progressive housing policies since late 2023.
Philanthropist Douglas Freeman pledged $20 million to build affordable housing units in low-income neighborhoods.
Federal resources such as the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) do not always meet demand, so state and local governments are experimenting with bond measures and housing funds.
Financial analyst Emily Chen cautions that bonds and housing funds must be coupled with cost-effective spending and long-term planning to keep affordable housing sustainable.
Urban planner Kevin Brooks says planning must cover transitional housing, single-occupancy units, family apartments, and accessible homes for people with special needs.
The city of Charlotte partnered with several private companies to fund and build mixed-income housing developments in revitalized neighborhoods.
The article cites smart technology and 3D-printed homes as innovations that could lower costs and speed up building.
